utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we'll start the administratively hearing on scheduling, there are a few procedural matters I would like to deal with. First, also about scheduling: Following the submissions by the parties in court yesterday with regard to the scheduling after the winter recess, the Chamber informs the parties that it will not be sitting on the 7th, the 8th, and the 9th of January, 2013, thereby including the day of Orthodox Christmas on the 7th of January. As of the 10th of January, 2013, the Chamber will sit as usual, following the normal pattern. We are still exploring the possibility if that is of any use to the Defence, perhaps early arrival, whether on the 10th there would be a possibility to move to the afternoon session. But if it does not accommodate the Defence, we'd like to know because then we'd stick to the usual schedule. Second, admission of associated exhibits tendered through Witness Tucker. The Chamber has received a revised list of associated exhibits. The Prosecution wants to tender -- the exhibits the Prosecution wants to tender following the end of yesterday's testimony of Witness Tucker. The Chamber will consider the Prosecution's request in light of its guidance and issue a decision after the two-week break. In this respect, the Chamber draws the parties' attention to transcript page 320, where it elaborated on the tendering of associated exhibits. If the Prosecution has any further submissions on this matter, the Chamber would like to receive them in writing by close of business tomorrow. The Defence should then respond by Monday, close of business. And just to clarify, the Chamber has invited the Defence not to unnecessarily invoke the guidance when responding to 92 ter motions. The mere fact, therefore, that there was no objection to the number of associated exhibits is in itself not a reason for the Chamber then to automatically admit them. I leave it to that. Then the next item on my list is pace of filing of 92 bis or 92 quater motions. On the 28th of September, 2012, Mr. Groome, you made a submission about increasing the pace of the filing of Rule 92 bis motions. The Chamber has previously indicated that these motions should be filed at least two or three weeks apart. Could the Prosecution please indicate what schedule it would prefer in order to have all its 92 bis and quater motions filed in a reasonable time before the close of its case. I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in essence, what the Prosecution was seeking to do was permission to file them as they are completed by us, recognising that it may -- doing it in that way may impose a burden on the Defence, but that we would have a standing position that we would not object to any application by the Defence seeking time under Rule 127 for additional time outside of the two weeks. It was the Prosecution's position - and it still remains that - that the sooner they are all before the Chamber and all before the Defence, a schedule could be developed for the Defence to respond. We believe that if the Chamber allows us to do it in this way and if the Chamber agrees that we can hold in abeyance the 29 witnesses that we gave notice of last week as well as the 19 witnesses that may -- we may not call depending on the decision of the Chamber on the bar table motion, we believe we could complete that process by the end of January/the beginning of February 2013.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we will consider it whether we would still expect the Prosecution to do it piece by piece or let's say small series by small series, or whether we would accept your submission. Has the Defence any specific position in relation to what Mr. Groome just said? Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. We stand by our earlier position. In view of the fact that we have to respond to two 92 bis motions already, we'd like to put it all in one filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly by "put it all in one filing"? What Mr. Groome suggests is that for responses to 92 bis motions, that additional time would be given for you to respond. But you now say that you respond in -- to put it all in one filing. Do you mean the Prosecution to put it all in one filing? Or the responses to be put in one filing? It's not clear, to me at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we announced in our discussions with the Prosecution, we will ask for an extension of limit for our response to the two motions, and as far as I understand there will be other motions coming in view of the Prosecution's intention to include witnesses under 92 -- rather, 92 bis witnesses, to include them as 92 ter. So we would like to compile it all in one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, it's still not entirely clear to the Chamber, but if you intend to say that you'd rather give one response after you'd receive all of the 92 bis filings and then of course have sufficient time for that, then the Chamber might not be that happy with it because we have to proceed as well. I mean, if you would respond, even if you take some additional time, if we would receive that response we could then decide. But if we would wait until all the 92 bis motions being filed and then to wait for a response for all of them in one filing, that would be -- that would impede our proceedings. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We understand, Your Honour, and that would exactly be our goal. According to the information we have, responses to five motions have already been provided. We are yet to provide two responses and we are prepared to respond to the future motions filed by the Prosecution. Of course -- so we know at some point where the whole process will end. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I think that the Chamber would be assisted if the Defence would indicate once it has received another 92 bis motion when the Defence thinks it could respond to that one, and of course you then take into account what the -- what the still outstanding portion of 92 bis motions is. That is accepted. I saw that there was nodding yes from the Defence side. Then a few very smaller matters. I think the record does -- is not clear on whether D74 has been admitted. I hereby put on the record that D74 is admitted into evidence. In relation to Witness RM145, on the 27th of September the Chamber invited the Defence in court to make written submissions in relation to the MFI's P257 and P258. These were video-clips related to events near Rajlovac. I take it that you have a recollection of that. The Chamber did not receive any submissions. Can the Chamber interpret this to mean that there are no further objections against admission of D257 and D258 -- P, P257 and P258.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. There are none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P257 and P258 are admitted into evidence and I think they should be under seal, but we'll verify that. Madam Registrar, if you would assist the Chamber in this respect, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also addressing the Prosecution. Madam Registrar tells us that they both were MFI'd as public exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Prosecution's position that there's no need for them to be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then P257 and P258 are admitted as public exhibits. A correction in relation to D72. When Exhibit D72 was admitted into evidence, it was announced as 1D313, which was a mistake. It should have been announced as 1D330. Now, since the e-court uploaded exhibit is the one that was admitted as D72, this correction is hereby on the record and there's no need for further action. Next item, submissions on D20, the NIOD report. The Chamber is still awaiting parties' submissions on D20, this report. When can we expect them?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye's more familiar with this particular exhibit. I'll ask him to address that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, when can the Chamber expect that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've actually communicated with the Defence and we've agreed on a position. I believe it would be pages 1 through 3 of that document and that would suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Pages 1, 2, and 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now what is uploaded in e-court as D20, that is more than the first three pages, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think the entire chapter is loaded into e-court right now. It's 14 pages, and we've agreed to tender -- or that the first three should constitute the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for my understanding I think D20 was MFI'd or was it already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe it was MFI'd pending an agreement with the Defence and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's my recollection as well, which means that once being MFI'd the Registry needs the approval of the Chamber to replace the earlier version by the three pages which now remain. Madam Registrar, is that -- have you received a new version just existing of three pages?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and currently we don't have anything in e-court under that number so the number was just reserved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could then be uploaded in e-court the three pages you just indicated the parties agreed upon as to be tendered under number D20. Once uploaded, D20, first three pages of the NIOD report is admitted into evidence. When will it be uploaded, Mr. Vanderpuye or Mr. Stojanovic? Yes, I think it's a D exhibit so it would be for the Defence to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. We agreed that they would be three pages. We will do it by Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's hereby on the record. Then the next and the last item on my brief agenda are the Tadic transcript references. On the 27th of September of this year, the Defence used excerpts of Witness Selak's testimony in the Tadic case which had been uploaded under 65 ter numbers 1D273 and 1D275. The transcript pages indicated on these excerpts did not match the official transcript pages. I hereby put on the record that the Defence informed Chamber's staff that there had been a mistake, which has been rectified, and that the correct excerpts have been uploaded under numbers 1D273A and 1D275A. No further action at this moment is required. This was all on my agenda. Mr. Groome, under number 9 it says "administrative hearing on scheduling." Would you like to -- we still have some time. Would you like to raise any matter in relation to scheduling?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to scheduling, the Prosecution on the 8th of October sent a draft to both Chamber staff and the Defence regarding the proposed scheduling for weeks 14 to -- sorry, weeks 11 to 14 which would take us up until the next adjournment and cover four weeks. The Defence have very gratefully -- or the Prosecution very much appreciates the estimates they've provided. We've taken that into account when we scheduled. So there's not a lot to discuss at this moment unless the Chamber after reviewing this document feels there should be some adjustments and would request the Prosecution to bring in witnesses prior to the time that they're now identified being available to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will further look into the matter but is now informed that there is no agreement between the parties on the scheduling as proposed by the OTP. We'll further consider it, and if we would have any problems I think we could inform the parties not any later than this Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then, Your Honour, there are two other matters that I'd like to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Karadzic Defence case will begin shortly, and the Prosecution has recently been able to access Karadzic Defence exhibits as they are currently being uploaded and released in the Karadzic e-court. We expect that this process will continue throughout Mr. Karadzic's case. We also expect that over the course of the Karadzic Defence case we may receive disclosures from him in other ways as well. There are approximately 8.000 exhibits on the Karadzic Defence exhibit list and a large number of witnesses who may testify. I raise this as a concern for the following reasons. First, there is a strong likelihood that given the nature of this material that a high percentage, if not all of it, will be material that the OTP must disclose under Rule 68. Second, it is likely to be a large volume of material. Third, the Karadzic Defence is commencing its case with a presentation of evidence related to Sarajevo; so in effect, the Prosecution in this case will be presenting its evidence related to Sarajevo at the same time in another case, material requiring disclosure is just becoming available to the Office of the Prosecutor to review and evaluate for disclosure. Obviously a process of the Office of the Prosecutor downloading these large e-court disclosures, organising, cataloguing, and reviewing this material would result in a delay of the Mladic Defence getting the material at the time it is most useful to them. The Prosecution thereby proposes to deal with this situation in the following way. I have spoken to the Mladic Defence, they are in agreement with this proposal. Given their agreement, I am not seeking any resolution of any issue at this time, but given the unusual nature of the situation and the importance of it, I believe it is prudent for the Chamber to be aware of the matter. The proposed resolution, Your Honour, is as follows, that the Prosecution has agreed to provide the Defence, the Defence has agreed to receive, material provided to the OTP by the Karadzic Defence as soon as we are able to copy it onto a hard drive. In essence, when we are able to access the material through e-court, we will duplicate it for the Mladic Defence. This will allow the Mladic Defence to have the material in the shortest amount of time and will allow them to incorporate it into their existing searchable library of disclosed materials. They will be able to exploit the material as quickly as possible. We anticipate being able to disclose approximately 6.000 of the Karadzic exhibits within the next two weeks. There are approximately 1.000 documents which may include material supplied by Rule 70 providers and we will have to take a closer look at these documents to ensure that we have permission to disclose them. Where we do not, we will undertake to get that permission. We will of course engage in a process of cataloguing and indexing this material. When that process is completed, we will place all of the material in a discrete, searchable index in the electronic disclosure system under Rule 68(ii). Of course if during the process of working with this material we encounter any material which places us in actual knowledge of potentially exculpatory information, we will bring that to the immediate attention of the Mladic Defence. Your Honour, when I looked at this issue I considered what relationship it might have to Mr. -- to a Defence access motion to the Karadzic case. In doing so, I was informed that the Mladic Defence, although it has sought access to many other Tribunal cases, has not sought access to confidential material in the Karadzic case. Given the parity that exists between the two cases, I wonder whether that is an oversight. Your Honour, there is also the possibility that OTP staff may interview Karadzic Defence witnesses prior to their testimony. It is likely that any notes of these interviews would constitute material that must be disclosed pursuant to Rule 68. We have implemented an OTP protocol with the Karadzic Prosecution team to ensure that these notes are provided to the Mladic Defence as quickly as possible. We will not be subjecting them to an internal review process, but we will simply disclose them given the high probability that they will contain material which must be disclosed and given the importance of avoiding any delay in the Mladic Defence receiving them. That concludes my submissions on that particular topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, I think Mr. Groome spoke more or less on behalf of both Prosecution and Defence since he said you had agreed on it. Anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Your Honour. We spoke about this yesterday with Mr. Groome, and I think that we agreed on that point. One issue remains open. Did the Defence ask for access to these documents in the Karadzic case? Well, we do believe that we have done so and we are still conducting searches that we hope will prove that we have done so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Groome, disclosure of course in another case is only allowed to the extent the material is not protected, confidential. Therefore, if it's done then the possible obstacle against full disclosure, that is, including confidential material - and I'm not talking about Rule 70 material - may be -- may have been addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: We'll be mindful of reviewing it for that purpose as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And seek any appropriate orders that we need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Having dealt with this matter, the Chamber expresses its appreciation for the parties to agree on how to proceed in this matter, which is indeed a bit extraordinary. Next point, Mr. Groome. You said you had two matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Chamber has expressed its preference for bar table motions to be filed at a time later in the Prosecution case. The Chamber did make exception with respect to one case recognising the potential benefit of the Prosecution filing a bar table motion regarding intercept evidence. And the Chamber agreed to receive that application at an earlier time. The Prosecution now wants to raise with the Chamber whether the Chamber would consider receiving another class of bar table motions earlier in the case. These bar table motions relate to some of the upcoming expert witnesses. The benefits of this, in our submission, would be that there would be a far clearer record of the expert's report and testimony if matters related to the admission of some of the exhibits the Prosecution intended to use and are incited in the report are referenced by their P number rather than an ERN number. Similarly, questioning in court could be done on the basis of P numbers instead of 65 ter numbers. In the alternative, the Prosecution would seek leave to file an application at least seeking that the documents an expert refers to be marked for identification, and there once again allowing the examination to proceed in a clearer, more efficient way. We would not do this for all experts, only for those which we think doing so would be clearer -- would be a clearer and more efficient way of presenting our case. For example, Dorothea Hanson is a Prosecution expert. Given the substance of her report and her expected testimony, we believe that much of her evidence may not be a matter of real dispute between the Prosecution and the Mladic Defence. We therefore think in the case of her expert evidence, it makes more sense to continue discussions with the Defence and wait until after her testimony before making a decision regarding what documents we should tender through a bar table motion. There are other experts, however, who it's clear their expert evidence will be a matter of great contention and we believe that it would assist the trial process in resolving the admissibility issues of documents relied on by those experts in advance of them appearing before the Chamber. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Groome. Is the Mladic Defence already in a position to respond to this suggestion to the Chamber to review its position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow us that possibility, we would like to have the time to express our views on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll consider it once we've received the response by the Defence. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, and there's one small residual matter regarding 65 ter 22719A. It is a video that arose during the evidence of Mr. Crncalo. The Prosecution understood from transcript page 3309 that the Defence wanted to review the material over the weekend and communicate their position regarding it on the 1st of October. I've asked Mr. Traldi to come to court today. If the Chamber considers it a productive use of time to deal with that now, we are prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is the Defence in a position to deal with 22719A?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I've just consulted with my colleague who cross-examined Mr. Crncalo, and in principle we are not going to oppose this, that is to say to have this video-clip admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, you'll forgive me for not having everything in my memory. Was it MFI'd already or --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was not MFI'd --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, if I remember correctly, this is a document that the Trial Chamber asked us to check. And if I'm not mistaken, it is a recording of a celebration that took place elsewhere, as it were, in relation to this witness. So it was not played in the courtroom. It was not tendered through the witness. So this is a pending issue, if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think the Chamber raised the matter, but in relation to evidence presented by the Defence. Therefore, the Defence is invited to upload into e-court 22719A, if need be with transcripts -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that you wanted to use a different number, which would then be 22719AA. Would you please upload that into e-court and since it is -- it's done already. It was in relation to evidence presented by the Defence. Do you intend to tender it now, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. At this point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that the material you said you would use with a future witness -- just talking about numbers, I think it was a speech delivered at a certain occasion by Mr. Seselj, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. We think that that is it exactly, and this speech did affect the conduct of this witness in a certain way. However, the Defence did not tender this, the Defence did not put it on its list. After hearing this witness, we made an effort to find this footage and to see what this was all about. As far as we're concerned, we are not going to tender this into evidence. However, we are not going to oppose any motion by the Prosecution, or rather, if the Prosecution wish to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and we would tender the material into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm prepared to address its authenticity and relevance, but it seems as if there's no dispute in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no dispute about it. There's no objection against it. Madam Registrar, is there any text and are there transcripts uploaded?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, there is a cover sheet and two transcripts, one B/C/S, one English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Then 22719AA will receive what P number? It's not on your 65 ter list, Mr. Traldi, but in view of the developments its admission would include here leave to add it to your 65 ter list. Madam Registrar, it would receive number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number P319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P319 is admitted into evidence, and it can be as a public exhibit if I am well informed. Any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That is all the matters that the Prosecution wanted to raise. We thank you for giving us the time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any other matter from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at this point in time, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break. Is -- would it -- would the Prosecution be ready to call its next witness at noon?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break and we'll resume at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, Ms. Bolton, we received a confidential Prosecution exhibits list. Second page, third from the top, 20799 I think is uploaded with an A, although that's not yet reflected on this list, intercepted telephone conversation. Two rows further down, 20805 appears on the list with an A and should be without, as it is at this moment in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's hereby on the record. Good morning, Mr. Wilson. Before you give evidence and could I invite you to stand for a second. The Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you. I would like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Wilson. Mr. Wilson, you'll first be examined by Ms. Bolton. Ms. Bolton is counsel for the Prosecution, and you'll find her to your right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Does the Court or does my friend have any objection to Mr. Wilson having a hard copy of his consolidated statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I usually do not intervene in translation issues, but I heard "nee" and it was interpreted "yes."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. It was barely audible. It sounded like a yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there's no objection, as I understand. Could a copy be provided to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask that 65 ter 28450 be brought up, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We're on page 1 of that document, sir. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is this a copy of the statement you provided to the Office of the Prosecution on the 29th of March, 2009?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask in the English version only, please, to turn to page 37 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you'll see before you there sir, a signature. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And have you had the chance recently to review your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And I understand there are a couple of corrections to be made?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There are.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The first, as I understand it, is with respect to paragraph 76 of the statement, where the - sorry - date on the first line should be the 29th of May, 1992, and not 1995?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Secondly, paragraph 91, the phrase "the same day" should read "the next day."

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And finally, in paragraph 95, I understand you actually drove back from Belgrade to Sarajevo, not Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And with those corrections, does your statement accurately and fairly reflect the information you provided to the Office of the Prosecutor in 2009?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if you were asked similar questions today to those that were posed to you in 2009, would your answers be substantially the same?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They would.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And now that you have taken a declaration of truthfulness, do you affirm the truthfulness of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'd seek admission of the statement under Rule 92 ter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 28450 becomes Exhibit P320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, Your Honour, may I read a summary of the witness's evidence into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: General John Wilson has evidence to give in respect of scheduled incident G1 before this Tribunal as well as a number of other matters. He retired from the Australian army in 1998 after 34 years of service. From January to November of 1992, General Wilson served first as the senior military liaison officer for the UNMLY and then as the chief military officer for the UNMOs. From mid-November 1992 until December 1993, General Wilson acted as the military advisor to the ICFY. And General Wilson was awarded the conspicuous service cross for his service in the Middle East and the former Yugoslavia. He provides evidence about the deteriorating situation in Sarajevo in March and April 1992, which culminated in the outbreak of hostilities. He will also give evidence about beginning to receive reports about ethnic cleansing by both the JNA and Serb militias, particularly in Bijeljina, Zvornik, and the Drina valley, as well as reports of the unlawful imprisonment of civilians in detention facilities. And I anticipate he will give evidence to the effect that he raised some of these issues with the Bosnian Serb leadership, including General Mladic. Between the 13th of May and the 24th of June, 1992, General Wilson was in the city of Sarajevo regularly and he witnessed frequent heavy bombardment of the city by the Bosnian Serb forces, which he will describe in his evidence. General Wilson has indicated that he's never seen such weight of fire used and particularly not against civilian targets. And he will give evidence of his observations of the disparity in terms of the Bosnian Serb forces and the Presidency forces in terms of armaments. In May 1992, General Wilson was involved in negotiations regarding the evacuation of JNA personnel from three barracks in Sarajevo. And during two of those meetings, I anticipate he will testify that General Mladic threatened to retaliate against the city of Sarajevo if the evacuation of the barracks did not proceed to his satisfaction and was not completed by May 28th. As indicated at the beginning, he will give evidence about the massive bombardment of the city on the May 28th to May 29th from Bosnian Serb artillery. And he will give evidence about conversations he had following those events with representatives of the Presidency and General Mladic, and particularly he will give evidence about an audio-recording he was played which purported to be of General Mladic directing the fire on May 28th and 29th. That's the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Bolton. Repeatedly you said that you anticipated the witness would give evidence. Since his statement is in evidence, there's nothing to expect anymore but rather what is already there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, force of habit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you have any further questions to the witness, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I do have some clarifying questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good morning, General Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Your background is set out in considerable detail in your statement, and so I have just a few questions for you. During the 35 -- or 34 years that you served with the Australian army, did you receive any training in the use and different kinds of artillery?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Initially during my four-year training to become an officer, we spent some weeks learning how to be a gunner on the gun-line and how to actually control the artillery on the gun-line. As I became an officer we received progressive training throughout my whole career on the employment of artillery, how it was to be targeted, its effect, the different ways of using it, the different places that one should use different types of artillery, and also in my military law training when you could use artillery and when you couldn't use it as a legitimate weapon of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And have you ever had occasion to command artillery formations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In my last command appointment immediately before I retired, I had an artillery regiment under my command in my brigade. A regiment is a unit of about 600 strong, 600 persons, with 12 artillery pieces in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what experience, if any, do you have with respect to the use and deployment of snipers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Every infantry battalion in the Australian army has a sniper section. These are highly specialised riflemen with sophisticated weapons. These soldiers are highly trained in concealment, in being able to observe and approach targets without being seen themselves. And you'd routinely expect them to be able to hit a target of a person size at a thousand metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Right. If I could just move on to paragraphs 5 and 6 of your statement. You speak in those paragraphs about the fact that when you were originally deployed to the former Yugoslavia you were part of the United Nations Military Liaison Officers Mission in Yugoslavia. What was the state of conflict at that time between the JNA and the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There was supposedly a cease-fire in effect from 1 January 1992, which had been negotiated by Mr. Cyrus Vance. The role of our small mission was to report to UN New York violations of that cease-fire, which took place along the confrontation line between the JNA and the Croatian forces, mainly in Croatia. At that time routinely between 2- and 300 violations were reported each day. These varied from perhaps one sniper to several hundred rounds of artillery being fired into an urban area within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Right. And I take it then that yourself and the other monitors were actually physically located near the border between Yugoslavia -- sorry, between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were 75 observers or liaison officers in total, half on each side of the line of confrontation, and they were deployed at the corps headquarters level of each of the parties and that is some distance behind the confrontation line. So they were not actually able to confirm the violations of the cease-fire which was reported to them. That was simply a post office.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You weren't in the city of Sarajevo, I suppose, is my point.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. The -- that mission had nothing to do with Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Right. And the mission then that commences in mid-March 1992 when the UNMOs are introduced into the former Yugoslavia, were any of the UNMOs at that point in time involved in any kind of active monitoring in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, the military observers from March 1992 had no role whatsoever under the Vance Plan and in Sarajevo. We did have some deployed in the area of Bihac and Mostar, but none in Sarajevo nor did we have a role there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You discuss in your statement at paragraphs 17 to 24 the system of reporting within the UNMO system. And my question is that as the chief monitoring officer for the UNMOs, were you privy to both the immediate and the formal reports you discussed in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to concentrate the next portion of my questions, sir, on your -- the time-period between the 13th of May, 1992, and the 24th of June, 1992, when I understand you were spending the bulk of your time in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I was actually residing in the city at that time, living in the PTT building and working out of there also.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And just to be clear, I understand that you were actually out of the region between the 30th of April, 1992, and the 13th of May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'd been given leave to return to Jerusalem to repatriate my wife back to Australia. I left her in Jerusalem while I was on temporary deployment in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And just to be clear, were you in Sarajevo when President Izetbegovic was kidnapped?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And were you involved at all in the negotiations surrounding either his release or General Kukanjac's release?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, I was not. These events took place while I was out of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to turn then to the date of your return to Sarajevo after you assisted your wife with repatriation, which I understand to be -- was it the 13th or the 14th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe it was the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And paragraphs 41 to 43 of your statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton. Ms. Bolton, both the French and the B/C/S booths are just able to cope with your speed of speech. If you would allow them to take a breath now and then as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My apologies to the booths.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, then at paragraphs 41 to 43 of your statement you indicate that there was some heavy fighting in the Dobrinja area of Sarajevo near your apartment on the 14th of May. Could you tell the Tribunal where you spent the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I actually spent the day in my apartment. It was virtually impossible to move outside the building on that day. In the Dubrovnik area there was very heavy infantry fighting. Armour was employed. And there was very heavy volume of mortar and artillery fire in that locality. Limited opportunity to observe outside the window because of the danger of attracting fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated in your answer there that you were describing events in the Dubrovnik area, which I understand is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Where was the artillery and mortar fire coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The fire appeared to be coming from outside the city into the area of Dubrovnik in -- I keep saying it, my apologies, into the area of Dobrinja. And it was very heavy and lasted from early in the morning, approximately 5.00, until well into the evening. Many hundreds of rounds of artillery would have landed in my vicinity during that day, and it was only one small area within the whole of Sarajevo which was subjected to that type of fighting and fire on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, are you suggesting then that there were other areas of Sarajevo that were also subjected to that type of fire that day?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There certainly were and the staff of UNPROFOR headquarters in particular were caught up in some very heavy infantry and artillery fighting in the Ilidza area where their staff accommodation was. No UN staff on that day were able to move about the city and the staff were not able to move from their accommodation to the headquarters building to do any work.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated that what you observed was that there was heavy infantry fighting. Who was involved in the fighting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Certainly in the area of Dobrinja there were a number of Presidency policemen with a number of young civilian-clad soldiers, I guess they were, who were fighting on the side of the Presidency. I was able to observe through my window infantry who were apparently Serbs that were dressed in uniforms, green uniforms, with helmets, that were supported by tanks, and now fighting in quite an organised and professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how -- in terms of weaponry, how well equipped were the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Serb forces appeared to be equipped as a normal, well-armed, military force supported by artillery, mortars, and tanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the Presidency forces, how well equipped were they in terms of weaponry?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They were lightly equipped with rifles, essentially, and perhaps some anti-tank rockets, a very light shoulder-fired weapon. Most of them were dressed in civilian clothes. They appeared to be in the process of getting organised as a military force. They were basically a rag-tag bunch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So in terms of the professionalism of the manner in which they were fighting, how would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Quite unorganised. Unprofessional would be my description of the BH forces at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you described in your answers quantities of artillery fire coming in from the perimeter of the city. Did you have any understanding as to where or which forces that fire was coming from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. It's my belief that artillery mortar fire was coming from Serb-held positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was that belief based on?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The rounds were actually landing in areas that were held by the government forces, and it's very -- a large volume of fire which could not have been produced by the Presidency forces at that time nor would they have any reason to be firing in those areas. That volume of fire could only be produced by the Serbs because of the amount of heavy weaponry that they possessed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Let's talk about that for a moment. You indicated in paragraph 48 of your statement that provided an estimate of Bosnian Serb forces having something in the vicinity of 200 artillery and mortar barrels they could direct at the city, and in addition having a large number of other weapons, including anti-aircraft weapons. Could you tell us how you came up with that number?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There are basically two ways I arrived at that estimate. Firstly, it was over a period of time to look at the effect of fire that had been produced on the ground and to look at the area that was being covered. And you can roughly work out where artillery unit fire units would need to be placed to achieve that effect. It's just then a mathematical extrapolation to work out the number of fire units you would need to have that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The second method I was able to use, I was -- I had the opportunity to observe a map down in the military headquarters of the Presidency military headquarters, and they had plotted on that what the location of the Serb fire units that they'd been able to identify. That map more or less confirmed my estimate of the number of Serb fire units.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: All right. And you indicated earlier in your answers that the volume of fire you observed could not have been produced by the Presidency forces at that time. And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: By "volume of fire," I really mean that the number of rounds that actually landed on the ground. In any given day in Sarajevo, there were some thousands of rounds being fired into the city at that time. And on particularly heavy days like the 28th of May or the 14th of May, there may well have been 5.000, between 5.000 and 10.000 rounds fired into the city over a period of 12 to 16 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated - sorry, sir - at paragraph 50 of your statement that the Presidency forces at that time didn't have a great number of heavy weapons. Are you able to put a number on and a calibre, perhaps, in the weapons that you believed they had or observed them to have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I certainly heard and observed them firing 82-millimetre mortars. I believe they probably had some 120-millimetre mortars. They had a few tanks. And I would guess that they had somewhere between 20 and 30 barrels, I'll call them, at that time in mid-May of 1992. That number, no doubt, grew over time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Given the observations that you've shared with us as to the skills and fighting of the Presidency forces and their what you call disorganisation and their lack of weaponry, did you form any impression as to how prepared the Presidency forces were to fight a war in May and June 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I would describe in May of 1992 the Presidency forces were getting organised. They were not a complete fighting force. They were lightly equipped. They had limited training. And they had had a long way to go before they would be a competent military force.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How about the Bosnian Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I would describe that as patchy. They had some clearly well-organised, disciplined, equipped forces; in other areas like village militias they were dressed in civilian clothes, lightly armed, and I suspect ill-disciplined.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You mentioned village militias. I'm just focusing on Sarajevo. Within Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I -- that applies equally to Sarajevo. There were small sort of, I guess, suburban village sort of groupings of people who responded to protect their immediate area, their village, their suburb, on the outskirts or on the perimeter of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: One of the things you mention in your statement - this is at paragraph 49 - is having had the opportunity at some point to visit the Serb positions and look down on the city, as you described it. When would that visit have occurred?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It occurred sometime after the airport had been opened in June/July of 1992. I went on a tour with the senior military observer in Sarajevo. We travelled from Lukavica up around towards Pale and to the north of Sarajevo. And we visited a number of Serb artillery concentration sites there, particularly those in the north and what I would describe as an excellent view of the city. They could physically from the firing positions look down on the city, see individual people and vehicles moving around. They had a very good opportunity to know exactly what they were firing at from those positions, although the control of artillery use usually affected by forward observers and they had plenty of opportunity to deploy those forward observers in areas that had excellent observation over the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what is the role of those forward observers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Forward observers role is to identify targets, to communicate them to the gun position, and to adjust the fire of the artillery as it lands on the ground so it is hitting the target that is desired. That's the normal way of controlling artillery, through a forward observer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You indicated that you visited a number of Serb artillery concentration sites. What do you mean when you're talking about a concentration site?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Part of the plan for the opening of the Sarajevo airport was that the heavy weapons of both parties would be concentrated into areas where they could be observed by military liaison officers. And it is these areas I'm referring to as concentration sites.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you tell us what manner of weapons you saw?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I certainly saw on that tour 122-millimetre artillery and 155-millimetre artillery. I'm also aware from the firing that the Serbs did into the city that they had in their possession 120-millimetre mortars, rocket launchers and anti-aircraft cannon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And not to move too far forward in time, but the idea that the weapons would be concentrated and the agreement, was it ever fully adhered to to the satisfaction of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what time-period are you talking about there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period immediately prior to and after the opening of the Sarajevo airport that weapons that were within range of the airport were concentrated into known sites where they could be monitored. I don't recall any complaints from my senior military observer that there was a lack of co-operation from either of the parties in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could turn to some of your observations of the shelling and sniping activity in Sarajevo in May and June 1992. This is a subject that is addressed in paragraphs 47 to 60 of your statement, and I just have some clarifying questions. Paragraph 51 of your statement you describe Bosnian Serb forces -- you indicate that mortar and artillery fire from the Bosnian Serb forces was usually in response to some threat posed by the Presidency forces, but their responses were "disproportionate and indiscriminately directed at the city." Could you describe what you mean by disproportionate and indiscriminate?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The general reaction or the general reaction of the Serbs to provocation as I would describe it was overreaction. It was the use of sledgehammer to crack a nut. So in the case of -- I give an example in my statement of a mobile mortar which I observed that fired perhaps two rounds of mortar fire out of the city; and in response perhaps a couple of hundred rounds of 122-millimetre and 155-millimetre artillery rounds were fired back in counter-battery fire. Now, this covered an area of perhaps a square kilometre in an urban area and was firing the target area of one truck.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you talk about it being disproportionate, are you referring to the number of shots or the kind of weapon that was used in response or both or neither?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm really referring to both in this case, that -- well, in most circumstances that it was a general bombardment of the city almost constantly between the 14th of May and the 23rd of June when I departed the city. It was rare to have a quiet day. So there was a constant background of artillery fire coming into the city, and along the lines of confrontation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, could I seek verification of whether I understood one of the answers well. You said when talking about the counter battery fire: "Now, this covered an area of perhaps a square kilometre in an urban area and was firing the target area of one truck." Do I understand the last part of the sentence to be that you said what was there to be targeted was of the size of a truck but the firing extended to a square kilometre covering that by far larger area? Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You've successfully decoded my thoughtology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just to make that clear, when you use the term mobile mortar, can you physically describe what you were actually seeing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It was an improvised arrangement where the Presidency forces mounted a mortar on the back of a truck, just a flatbed truck so that it could fire and be very quickly redeployed. Normally mortars are fired from a metal base plate on the ground. They can be quickly redeployed, but it involves manhandling them, loading them onto a vehicle, and driving them away. It takes longer than operating from a back of a truck, as they had done. They were simply making it a much harder target for the Serbs to respond to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you had been -- well, sorry, what might have been an appropriate weapon to use in trying to hit a mortar that was mounted on a truck that was capable of moving?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: My point here about the disproportionate nature of the fire was that the actual procedure of responding with that type of weapon and that volume of fire against the military position outside a city would be perfectly normal military procedure. But here we've got this sort of very destructive fire being fired into an urban area which is going to cause -- it's quite clear it's going to cause quite a lot of collateral damage and potentially civilian casualties. So one has to sensibly seek other ways of perhaps countering this threat. And the Serb forces had at their disposal a large number of direct-fire weapons which -- perhaps like tanks or anti-aircraft weapons which if deployed forward and if they can see the target, they fire directly at it and are highly effective. They could have placed perhaps more emphasis on that. But the standard response was to fire a large number of heavy-calibre weapons into an urban area.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in this instance, what part of the city was that mobile mortar in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It was deployed between the PTT building and the city centre, about 1 and a half to 2 kilometres away from the PTT. I was observing the activity through binoculars from the top of the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On a related issue you discuss in your statement occasions when UNPROFOR would fire mortars not mounted on trucks but regular mortars from proximity to the PTT. How many times do you recall seeing that happen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: On at least one occasion the Presidency forces used the PTT building as a sort of cover so they could fire mortars out into Serb areas, and we had them on agreement with the Presidency forcibly removed from that location. It only happened once while I was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I seek clarification, Ms. Bolton. Madam Bolton, your question referred to fire by UNPROFOR. The answer is talking about fire by Presidency forces. What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, that was my error, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The mortars that we were talking about being fired in proximity to the PTT building, those were being fired by Presidency forces, not UNPROFOR; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did you raise that issue with the Presidency at all?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was they who actually arranged to move them on. We saw no benefit in having a confrontation with them over this particular deployment. But they were moved with -- they were moved quickly by the Presidency once they were aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We've heard some allegations that the Presidency forces may have positioned mortars in proximity to hospitals. If true, is that permitted by the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It is. I did receive reports of this happening and no, it's not permitted within the Geneva Conventions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Would that then entitle the Bosnian Serb forces to fire back without -- at the hospital without regard for the risk of civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I don't believe it does. I don't think two rights make a wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, despite the fact that there was no objection from the Defence, aren't you asking at this moment legal opinion?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm asking questions based on this witness's training in the area of the Geneva Conventions and military law, which he gave us some information about at the opening, and based on the jurisprudence of the Tribunal which has indicated in previous cases that people with military experience may give opinions based on their knowledge and experience and obviously -- on matters such as this. And obviously the ultimate decision on that issue lies with the Trial Chamber, but my understanding is the jurisprudence allows people like General Wilson to express the opinion and it's up to the Trial Chamber ultimately to determine the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the Chamber -- it is not only legal opinion but it is also to some extent expert opinion and just is it allowed or not of course does not explore the case law and the reasons why this witness has formed that opinion. So therefore, it's not the preferred way to receive this type of evidence. Could you please keep that in the back of your mind when you continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honours. I would just note that this issue was vetted somewhat in the pre-witness filings. It was an issue that was raised by the Defence in their response to our 92 ter filing, and we filed a reply to that which the Trial Chamber indicated by way of e-mail it was going to consider. And subsequently, there was the ruling that has been referred to by -- in the last couple of days on I believe it was the 6th of September, 2012, regarding -- guidance regarding 92 ter litigation, where the Defence were advised that they shouldn't keep raising the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- opinion evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not in response to the motion, but not that the matter would not be relevant anymore. Some -- of course to some extent we had given guidance in our earlier decisions and not to repeat again and again and again. I said that this is not a preferred way and whether you'd keep that in the back of your mind. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, one of the last things you said there was I think two rights don't make a wrong.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how about two wrongs making a right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, but can I comment that it's -- a military commander in this situation, certainly in Western military organisations, you would have a military lawyer there with you who would be advising you on targeting. And if there was any doubt about the legitimacy of a target, then you would be seeking advice from that lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I guess what I'm not clear on is -- I'll move on. Paragraphs 56 of your statement you indicated that during the six weeks you were in Sarajevo in May and June 1992 there was heavy artillery fire directed at virtually the whole of the city. And I just wish for you to clarify which force or forces was responsible for that heavy fire?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, I was able to observe fire coming into the city. That's where I was residing and I was really outside the city so I couldn't see any fire that may have been generated by the Presidency forces, though I am aware that they did on at least one occasion attack with mortars the Lukavica barracks. In general, the outgoing fire from the Presidency was light. The incoming fire from the Serb forces was constant, heavy, and widespread.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you refer to "widespread," what are you referring to there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, we were able to observe a considerable area of the city but not the whole city from the PTT. We had people positioned on the roof of a fairly tall building, you could see quite a way. And you could see artillery fire landing all around the PTT, in every direction. And you could certainly hear it. It was a constant background noise for the whole -- for virtually the whole period we're talking about. And it was heavy. It was -- would start early in the morning at perhaps 5.00 and it would run until sometime around about midnight.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you spoke about -- earlier about the fact that fire was often in return to some kind of a provocation. Where would the fire from the Serb forces be -- or was there any correlation between where the fire from the Serb forces was landing and where those provocations had come from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The UN was rarely in a position to observe the provocations as reported by the Bosnian force, but we would be told by the -- perhaps the Serb representatives that an infantry attack had been launched by the Presidency forces somewhere along the line of confrontation. The response to that attack would be artillery fire in the immediate area of the attack, but also in great depth behind that attack into the city where there were no apparent targets, military targets.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At paragraph 57 you describe: "I've been involved in conventional military operations as a soldier and I'd never seen such weight of fire used and particularly not against civilian targets." Where else had you been involved in conventional military operations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: As a young officer, a platoon commander, I was deployed in Vietnam on a regular basis, used artillery in support of operations there, including on one occasion calling it -- the fire down to within 100 metres of my men. I'd also been able to observe Israeli use of artillery in southern Lebanon and also in the Beirut area. And of course I could see the effects of the use of artillery in Croatia immediately after I arrived in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You speak in paragraphs 55 and 56 of your statement about the fact that shelling was a common occurrence and that there were a number of civilians killed by artillery or mortars apparently fired from Serb positions during the time-period. And my question is: Were you aware of any civilian deaths or injuries from Serbian snipers during May and June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We regularly received reports from the Presidency about civilian casualties. We certainly saw on the local TV actual film of people -- civilians being shot. And we received incidental reports from people travelling or from local employees. So we were aware that there were constant flow of casualties in the city at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at that juncture were there any areas in particular that the sniper -- Bosnian Serb sniper activity seemed to be concentrated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I did not travel throughout the whole city, but certainly on -- in the down-town, in the city area that was quite prevalent or on the fringes on it, and around Dobrinja it was very dangerous to move around that area also. But in travelling through the city we would routinely have our vehicles fired upon. I can't accuse any particular side of doing that. I believe both sides were guilty of firing on UN vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you travelled in UN vehicles to the down-town area of Sarajevo, would you travel along the main road that runs in front of the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, that was far too dangerous. One would use back streets and try and keep out of areas that were regularly observed or were subjected to fire. Even that precaution wouldn't stop you being fired upon. I would estimate that 70 to 80 per cent of the time we would receive fire against our vehicles when we were moving about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I'm looking at the clock. Would this be a suitable time for a break?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It would, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first have the witness escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, two observations in relation to the legal opinion. First of all, the standard response by the Defence often was this is expert opinion not within the limits of what a witness could tell us and we need an expert report. That's one. Now, this is of course a very specific expertise, that's legal expertise, which is of course within the knowledge of the Chamber and within the knowledge of the parties. So the witness without further elaborating on case law or what -- I mean, you would expect him to write a brief on the matter in order to be able to follow whether his opinion is valid or not. And that's really -- really we don't need that from this witness even if he had received some courses in the law of war. Second, you were specifically asking about whether the Geneva Conventions admit firing from the proximity of a hospital area. Is there any dispute about the illegality about such firing between the parties? I would be surprised as a matter of fact. The Prosecution apparently takes the position that it's not permitted under the Geneva Conventions. And I hardly could imagine that the Defence would take any other position. I see nodding that the Defence agrees. So therefore, it's a matter which is not in dispute, therefore no need to ask the witness questions about it apart from the whole aspect of legal opinion and expert evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I understand Your Honour's rulings and I will avoid these areas in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and we resume at 25 minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: General Wilson, just before we leave this topic, you had indicated in your statement that you would sometimes raise these issues with General Mladic - and I'm referring to incidents in which civilians were injured by or killed by either artillery fire or sniping fire - and that he would generally not deny responsibility but would provide a justification such as defending the Serbs or responding to attacks. Was there ever an occasion when you protested a civilian casualty to General Mladic that he seemed uninformed of the incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No. In particular, I had a meeting with him on the 30th of May, at which the events or the shelling of the city on the night of the 28th of May was discussed at some length. And he didn't deny responsibility or argue about the detail of the attack on that night. He accepted that he was responsible for it, but that he was acting in response to provocations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And we will come to that incident to discuss it in more detail in just one moment. Could we turn to the issue now of the evacuation of the JNA barracks which you discussed starting at paragraph 67 of your statement. There you indicate that there were three barracks to be evacuated and that this is one of your key activities after the 17th of May, 1992. Do you recall the names of the barracks that were to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do, although my pronunciation may be found wanting, but they were in the sequence in which they were evacuated. They were Viktor Bubanj, Jusuf Dzonlic and Marsal Tito.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who or what was inside the barracks that needed to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were JNA soldiers and in some cases their families were located inside the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was there any military equipment in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, there was. I didn't personally observe it, but I was led to believe that they were the personal weapons belonging to the soldiers and there was also an array of more heavy weapons which were the subject of lengthy and intense negotiations between the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who or what was preventing the troops and their families within the barracks from simply leaving?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The Presidency forces had invested the three barracks, were preventing anybody entering or leaving the barracks. They had barricades placed around them and in some cases they were denying them electricity and water.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 10613. And, for the record, this is a document the witness discusses at paragraph 71 of his statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We're seeing page 1 of this document in both English and B/C/S. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Who authored this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure who authored it. It would have been somebody in UNPROFOR headquarters in Belgrade, but it's released and signed by General Nambiar, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 1 you'd agree with me that there's an indication that there are some cables attached that were authored by yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I have page 7 in both English and B/C/S, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, there's a signature on this document in the English version. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the date appears to be the 20th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 1 refers to a meeting with General Mladic and Colonel -- is it Cadjo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Cadjo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Taking place at the Lukavica barracks. Were you in attendance at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who is Colonel Cadjo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Colonel Cadjo was the JNA liaison officer to UNPROFOR. He was with UNPROFOR before they deployed to Sarajevo and remained until after the last barracks was evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And at paragraph 2 there's an indication that the general stated there was a shortage of food - I'm paraphrasing - in the Viktor Bubanj --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Bubanj, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Barracks, I assume. Who is the general they're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can we scroll down so that paragraph 3 is visible in both English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, there is a discussion in paragraph 3 (A), (B), and (C) of an agreement between reached between the Presidency and presumably General Mladic for the delivery of some food to the Viktor Bubanj barracks, and also in subparagraph (C) to some food being delivered to the children's embassy convoy. Could you describe what the children's embassy convoy references to.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: At that time there was convoy of approximately 2.000 who the humanitarian organisations were attempting to evacuate out of Sarajevo to the coast. They were being prevented from leaving the city by the Serb forces and were being used as a bargaining tool to get concessions from the Presidency forces in -- associated with the evacuation of the three barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Where were they being held up?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe they were being held in the vicinity of Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who was using them as a bargaining chip?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Ultimately it was General Mladic who was preventing their passage from the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Because this cable records a discussion that was going on between the Presidency and General Mladic through us which various concessions were being sought by both sides. The Presidency was seeking the release of the children's convoy and General Mladic wanted to affect the evacuation of the Viktor Bubanj barracks. The movement of food was a preliminary action before the actual evacuation of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we please have in the English version paragraph 4, so the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's an indication there at paragraph 4 that during the discussions on that date the general also mentioned that if a peaceful solution for the evacuation of personnel from the barracks could not be found, he would use other methods and threatened to destroy half the city. Again, who is the general we're referring to there?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
