utterances.text: In this case we're referring to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what city did you understand General Mladic to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did he indicate or intimate how he would destroy half the city?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: He indicated that he would use considerable artillery resource that he had at his disposal. He talked about levelling half the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you take his threat seriously?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I always took General Mladic's statement seriously. He was known to deliver what he said, both good and bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that this be marked as the next exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would you please ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be Exhibit P321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P321 is admitted into evidence in the absence of any objections. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 09382, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, you should see a document before you. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It appears to have been authored by an Adnan Abdelrazek. Who is that gentleman?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. Abdelrazek was the civil affairs officer allocated to Sarajevo when the UNPROFOR headquarters relocated to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what country was he from?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: He was a displaced Palestinian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, is it that you want to elicit evidence for us to know?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I simply want -- I was going to ask the witness to clarify that this is not the same Abdelrazek as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that's then well done. I intervened too early, apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And, sir, is this the same individual or a different individual than General Husein Aly Abdel-Razek of Egypt?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Different personalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At paragraph 4 of this document - if we could just scroll down, please - there is again a reference to a convoy of 2.000 women and children. Is this the same or different convoy than we were discussing in terms of the children's embassy convoy?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The same convoy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in terms of the contents of this document, if we could turn in English, please, to page 2, so paragraph 5. There's an indication there that you ended up issuing an order suspending mobile assistance by UNPROFOR for humanitarian or other purposes. Why was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: In the preceding week or so we had been consistently fired upon with considerable violence when moving about the city and had reached the stage where there was absolutely no respect for the UN presence there. And I did this to draw the attention of the leadership of both sides to the fact that it was impossible to operate under those circumstances. They had to impose some sort of authority if we were to continue to be able to work. It was simply an attention getter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And did it assist you at all in moving forward negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Well, the leadership was certainly willing to co-operate, but there was still elements of ill-disciplined, elements within the city continued to fire upon us, but there was a slight improvement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, you'd indicated that there was a bargaining process ongoing with respect to the JNA barracks on the one hand and the children's convoy on the other hand. You've had the opportunity to review this document during proofing?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And does this document accurately reflect how or what transpired with respect to those events?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Ultimately were the children safely allowed to proceed on their way?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And who delivered on that promise?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It was an agreement from General Mladic that they be allowed to proceed on the basis that food was actually delivered to Viktor Bubanj barracks. And I physically delivered that food to allow that release to take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And on the previous page had there been an indication that the convoy was being held by Serbian militias. Did you draw any conclusion about General Mladic's ability to control those militias in terms of holding the children or releasing the children?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: They were being held on his authority. He made it quite clear on a number of occasions that he "controlled everything."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that that document be introduced as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter 09382 will be Exhibit P322.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In your statement you indicated -- we started to talk about the fact that you were attending negotiations over the evacuation of the JNA, and could you tell me was the JNA represented in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA was represented by a number of different leaders, but primarily by General Boskovic, who I believe was an air force officer with some intelligence portfolio.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And was the Presidency represented in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: By whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Principally by Mr. Djorko, who was the Defence minister, I believe, and assisted on many occasions by Mr. Pusina, who I think was deputy minister for the interior, a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the Bosnian Serbs, were they represented?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, they weren't, although they were consulted by the JNA representatives on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were you aware as a result of your discussions with any of these parties of any areas of disagreement between the JNA and General Mladic with respect to the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, there was a violent disagreement on the issue of handing over of weapons from the JNA to the Presidency forces. I was made aware of this both by observing the negotiations, by being briefed by the JNA representatives, and talking with General Mladic about the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recall what roughly the position of the Presidency was with respect to the weapons inside of the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The Presidency were insisting that all heavy weapons within the barracks should be left behind, and they were also arguing that they should have a percentage. I believe it was something like 60 per cent of light weapons should be returned to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And as these talks progressed in terms of the evacuation, could you tell us were the media present during any of these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, the media were not present and they were not informed about the progress of negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And in particular were the details of the plans once reached for evacuation a matter of public knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 27571, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is a transcript of an intercepted conversation where the speakers have been identified as a Captain Tomcic and Ratko Mladic with a date of the 21st May, 1992. And you'll see that the conversation begins with speaker identified as Ratko Mladic saying: "Yes." Tomcic saying: "This is Captain Tomcic here."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- no loud speaking. No loud speaking. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And within the first five lines you will see that the speaker identified as Ratko Mladic says: "This is Mladic speaking."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down, please. Thank you. I guess in both -- the B/C/S as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's then a conversation where General Mladic is asking: "Do you have enough food?" And they're discussing the fact that there is bread and there are beans for lunch. And General Mladic cautions them to distribute or Tomcic to distribute it evenly. And then finally you'll see in the last fourth and fifth last lines there's a reference to: "Don't let them approach you by vehicles. Are there any barracks around the barracks?" This is a 21st of May, 1992. Do you recall whether at that point in time food had yet to be delivered to the Viktor Bubanj barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I believe it was delivered on the 21st, but I may well be wrong on that -- 21st or 22nd, somewhere around there the food was actually delivered, but it was linked to the release of the children's convoy and the food was delivered before the convoy was released.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there any other barracks in the Sarajevo area at that time where food was an issue that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It was not raised with us that other barracks had a food problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 2 in both documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And while they're bringing up the document, to the best of your knowledge was the fact that there was a short supply of food in the barracks of Viktor Bubanj, was that a matter that was a matter of public knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't have been. It was certainly something that General Mladic raised with me. He had some concern that food ought to be provided to the Viktor Bubanj barracks while the negotiations progressed. There was also the issue of a sick soldier on the other side and I believe who had appendicitis. He was also evacuated as part of the bargaining process. When the food was delivered we removed the sergeant and delivered him back to Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On the English transcript approximately nine lines down you will see General Mladic referring to firing incendiary munitions that would burn the buildings down. What is an incendiary munition?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's a type of munition that typically white phosphorous thick and start a fire and burn a building down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you see white phosphorus or were you aware of white phosphorus being used by the Bosnian Serb forces while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I saw it being fired but I didn't see it being fired in an urban area. I saw it being fired on the hills around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No consultations during the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Moving further down on the page in the English version to the very bottom. General Mladic is quoted as saying: "So tell your men, because entire Sarajevo is blocked. There's nothing they can do. They can only breathe and birds can fly round Sarajevo." How does the description that General Mladic provides there accord with your recollection of the situation in Sarajevo at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: He's accurate in that the city was invested and it was very difficult for anybody to come in or leave the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could we have page 3 in both the English and the B/C/S, please. And could we scroll a little further down in the English page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's a reference about halfway down the page in English to snipers with silencers. Do you understand what that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: He's asking the young commander there whether he has soldiers equipped with sniper rifles which also have a silencer fitted. And the answer is that they do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And then the second-last line from the bottom that's visible on the screen there's a reference to passive night optics, it appears. What would that be a reference to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It's equipment that gives the use of the ability to see at night, quite often infrared. At that stage it wouldn't have been very sophisticated but enough to see people moving in close proximity to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The user of what?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You said it would allow the user to --

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: To observe any movement in the close vicinity of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the question is the user of what piece of equipment?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Of the infrared -- of the night vision equipment.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that that be tendered as the next exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter 275 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. I see Mr. Petrusic is on his feet. Mr. Petrusic, as that may have been caused by -- that you have to wait for the translation. Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not receive any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can you hear us now? There's been a breakdown in equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can hear you now. Could you please repeat your objection, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the position of the Defence in terms of the admission of intercepts from audiotapes is the following. We oppose that vehemently because authenticity has not been proven at all, namely that Mr. Mladic is one of the participants in this conversation. So the Prosecutor did not proffer any proper evidence in this respect. This is our general position with regard to all of these intercepts. As far as I can remember, the Defence is supposed to state its views one of these days in respect of all the intercepts that are to be used in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My respectful submission would be at this point I'm content -- there is going to be additional evidence led in these proceedings with respect to provenance. So I'm content that it be MFI'd for the time being if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection against the document being MFI'd? Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, this document would receive what number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 27571 will be P323 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status for the time being. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Earlier in your evidence you gave evidence about the fact that the city of Sarajevo was to repeated and almost continuous bombardment between the middle of May and the end of June 1992. Were there ever periods of quiet or respite from the bombardments?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: There were very few periods where it was quiet, but one notable occasion was the day on which the Marsal Tito barracks were evacuated. There was an eerie quiet throughout the whole city on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Not to spoil the story, but were the other two barracks eventually evacuated, Viktor Bubanj and Jusuf Dzonlic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, they were in a period of relative quiet, but not as quiet as the Marsal Tito evacuation day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 27576, please. And if we could scroll up in English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, this is an intercepted conversation where the speakers change, but you'll note that the date is the 24th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could we then have page 3 in both English and B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You'll note, sir, that near the top of the page there's the beginning of a conversation where there's introductions given. One person says: "Hello." And the other speaker says: "Mr. Doko ..." And the person says: "My respects!" And then the other person says: "Mladic, the general." Mr. Doko, his first name appears to be Jerko, is that an individual that's known to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: He was the Presidency minister of defence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could then turn to page 6 in both versions. And could we scroll down, please, to the bottom of the page in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, on the 24th of May, 1992, could you tell us if you recall what the situation was in terms of the Viktor Bubanj barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the date, the 24th?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The barracks were evacuated on that day, my understanding. I was actually out with the children's convoy at that time and some of my military observers were present during the evacuation of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: General Wilson, I thought you mentioned the name of the government, but it's not on the script. This gentleman whom you say is the minister of defence is the minister of defence of which government?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the BiH Presidency, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I did think you did say "Presidency."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: On the screen you'll see that General Mladic is quoted as saying at one point during this conversation: "I've not ordered one bullet to be fired at Sarajevo yet. I made fire around Sarajevo cease."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page in English, please. And I believe it's also the next page in B/C/S. Apparently not. If we could go back, please, I think it's just at the very bottom of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You will see that Ratko Mladic is quoted as saying: "Mr. Doko, you should know ..." And this is about a fifth of the way down the page: "... Sarajevo is within the range of my artillery. "You should also know that I now have more artillery pieces around Sarajevo than there were soldiers when I came over here." And then later on that page he says: "And, Mr. Doko, you know, ... let me just tell you ... "... your head is in front of my feet, not the other way around." Now, first of all, General Mladic is quoted as mentioning something about making Sarajevo or fire around Sarajevo cease. Had fire around Sarajevo ceased to any extent?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: The -- on the 24th there was sufficient quiet to allow the evacuation of the barracks so it was relatively quiet, but there was not total cease-fire within the city. To be honest, a cease-fire requires the co-operation of both parties; that was not always the case in Sarajevo. But certainly General Mladic was capable of imposing a cease-fire if he really wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what makes you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Because he did on occasions, most notably during the evacuation of the Marsal Tito barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The other thing that General Mladic is quoted as saying is that he has more artillery than men when he came to Sarajevo. Do you have any comment to make in respect of whether that was true or not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I received reports from my military observers later in 1992 that the Serb forces actually moved gun crews by bus between the various firing positions because they had more guns than they had men to fire them, so I guess that supports the statement by Mr. Mladic -- General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that that be marked as the next exhibit for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no objections against the document being MFI'd, Madam Registrar, the number would be ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter 27576 will be P324 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were there any major difficulties with the evacuation of the Viktor Bubanj barracks?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, it went relatively smoothly. There were some problems with the delivery of food but we'd learnt a lesson from there that there needed to be representatives of both parties at the site to make sure that things went smoothly. So the evacuation on the 24th went relatively smoothly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Now, according to your statement on the 25th of May, 1992 - and this is at paragraph 72 - you attended a meeting at the Lukavica barracks with General Mladic and Mrs. Plavsic. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could I have 65 ter 21363, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And while that's being brought up let me ask you: At that point in time how safe was it for the United Nations to move around the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We were still drawing firing on a regular basis. In particular when we moved between Dobrinja and Lukavica we would routinely be fired upon then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And had you taken any steps to try to make arrangements before going to Lukavica to ensure the safety of your voyage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We had liaison officers from both sides residing with us in the PTT building by this time. We would routinely advise them well in advance of our planned movements and we would ask them to warn their forces in that locality that we would be moving through and that we should be offered safe passage. I presume they did that but didn't necessarily stop the incidents of fire against our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You have before you a transcript of a conversation that purports to be between General Mladic and Colonel -- or Cadjo. Do you know who that individual is?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: He's the JNA liaison officer we discussed earlier in my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you'll note that there is an indication that someone from UNPROFOR who they quoted as Willston was to attend an appointment at your place that day at 1300 and then at the very bottom of the page in English that individual and asking General Mladic if he could prevent people from shooting in the area of Nedzarici as the convoy will be travelling through there today. Did you travel through the area of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: We did on a regular route that we used. I can't recall whether we were fired upon on that particular day or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you had been fired upon on that day, is that something that would be recorded in your -- in the reports that you submitted?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that this be introduced as the next document for MFI, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 21363 will be P325 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And keeps that status at this moment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: May I have 65 ter 03275, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, General Wilson?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I do. It's a report signed by myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And does that mean that you authored it if you signed it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: I authored it and released it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this is -- the subject matter is a record of discussion with Mrs. Plavsic and Lieutenant-General Mladic 25th May, 1992. And at paragraph 2 there is a quote that -- excuse me, there's a discussion of the evacuation of the remaining JNA personnel from the Sarajevo barracks. And then General Mladic is quoted as saying -- I'm sorry, who is the person who says: "The evacuation had to be completed in three days or strong action would be taken against Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: General Mladic made that statement. He was becoming frustrated that the negotiations of the evacuation of the barracks were protracted and not moving and there was little prospect of the barracks being evacuated quickly. And he was making it clear to me and asked me to pass on to the Presidency and, indeed, the Secretary-General that unless the barracks were evacuated soon that he would be taking strong action himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was Mrs. Plavsic present when this remark was made?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, she was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was her reaction?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: She had no objection to what Mr. Mladic -- or General Mladic had to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did he give any indication of why it had to be three days?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: No, he didn't. But he made it quite clear that if the barracks were not evacuated within three days that he would be taking strong action.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 discusses "international military intervention could only bring catastrophe on Sarajevo as, in a military option, Sarajevo would" I assume it should "be levelled." Who made that remark?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: General Mladic made that remark. There was some discussion in the international media at that time that there could be some international military intervention in the conflict. He was simply warning that the consequences of such intervention would be significant and in particular directed against the UN.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, just in terms of the remark that Sarajevo would be levelled, who did you understand would level Sarajevo if there was international military intervention?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: My understanding was that General Mladic would initiate artillery fire that would produce that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you just indicated moments ago that there was some kind of a warning about intervention directed against the UN. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: He pointed at the badge on my beret and said that's the badge of death if there is any foreign intervention in this conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And what was the badge on your beret?

utterances.speaker: JOHN WILSON
utterances.text: It was the UN badge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that that be marked as the next exhibit, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar, the number ... ?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 03275 will be Exhibit P326.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P326 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That would be a convenient place for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness already be escorted out of the courtroom but only after I've instructed you, Mr. Wilson, that you should not speak or communicate in any other way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given today or still to be given in the days to come. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perfectly clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, how much time would you need tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm right on schedule for my three-hour total estimate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means somewhere during the first session or immediately after the first session tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we adjourn for the day. We will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 11th of October, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of October, 2012, at 9.30 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.14 p.m.,
